title: Alternative Views on Gradient Sensing
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through two mathematical accounts of how a chemotactic cell — an amoeba such as *Dictyostelium* or a crawling neutrophil — reads a shallow external chemical gradient and turns it into an internal signal that points toward the source, without becoming permanently, irreversibly locked onto one direction. The two accounts are Postma and van Haastert's diffusion-translocation model (*Biophys. J.* 81, 2001) and the local-excitation/global-inhibition style model associated with Levchenko and Iglesias (*Biophys. J.* 82, 2002); it assumes familiarity with reaction-diffusion equations, steady states of ODEs and PDEs, and basic receptor–ligand binding. ## The problem: sensing without freezing A crawling cell sitting in a gradient of chemoattractant does not see a large difference in ligand concentration between its front and its back — for a cell of ordinary size the difference across the cell can be only a few percent. Two things have to happen for chemotaxis to work: the cell has to detect which end has the higher concentration, and it has to act on that by polarising — building up signalling machinery preferentially at the front. Both models below are built around a constraint on top of that: **polarisation has to be reversible.** If the readout locked onto a direction permanently, the cell could never follow a gradient that changes direction, or unlearn a front once it had moved past the source. Both solve this by making the readout a *relative*, adapting quantity rather than an absolute one. ## How far can a diffusing signal travel before it forgets its origin? Take the simplest possible description of a signalling molecule $m$ inside the cell: it is produced at rate $P$, diffuses with diffusion coefficient $D_m$, and is removed (degraded, or switched to an inactive form) at rate $k_{-1}$ per molecule: $$\frac{dm}{dt} = D_m \frac{\partial^2 m}{\partial x^2} - k_{-1} m + P$$ Diffusion coefficients for the two obvious classes of second messenger differ by roughly two orders of magnitude: a protein or lipid confined to the membrane diffuses at $D_m \sim 1\ \mu\text{m}^2 \text{s}^{-1}$, while a small molecule free in the cytosol diffuses at $D_m \sim 100\ \mu\text{m}^2 \text{s}^{-1}$ — membrane species are slowed by the bilayer, cytosolic ones are not. If production is switched on at one point and the molecule is left to diffuse and decay, the resulting steady profile does not spread indefinitely: balancing diffusive spreading against first-order removal gives a characteristic **dispersion length** $$\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{D_m}{k_{-1}}},$$ the distance over which the profile decays (this is the same balance that gives an exponential decay $e^{-x/\lambda}$ as the solution of the homogeneous version of the equation above). For a messenger to carry any information about *where* inside the cell it is made — for its steady profile to still look graded — that decay length has to be shorter than the cell itself, $\lambda \lesssim L$. In numbers, with $k_{-1} = 1\ \text{s}^{-1}$ and a cell size $L = 10\ \mu\text{m}$: the membrane species gives $\lambda \sim 1\ \mu\text{m}$, comfortably inside the cell — it can hold a spatial profile. The cytosolic species gives $\lambda \sim 10\ \mu\text{m}$, the size of the cell itself — something that diffuses that fast relative to its own turnover is essentially well-mixed before it decays, and cannot hold a gradient. This is why both models below build their spatial readout around a slowly-diffusing, membrane-associated species rather than a free cytosolic one. ## Passing the gradient through: the gain is less than one Now let the *production* of the messenger track the external signal directly. Receptor occupancy varies roughly linearly across the cell in a shallow gradient, so let $$\frac{dm}{dt} = D_m \frac{\partial^2 m}{\partial x^2} - k_{-1} m + P(x), \qquad P(x) = k_R\left(\bar R^* - \Delta R^* \frac{x}{r}\right).$$ Solving this at steady state, the internal profile of $m$ across the cell comes out shallower than the input profile: diffusion always flattens whatever spatial structure production tries to build, because it is a smoothing process — it moves material from wherever it is locally concentrated toward wherever it is locally scarce. The ratio of output steepness to input steepness (the *gain*) comes out less than 1, and the faster the messenger diffuses the smaller that gain is. A cell that only had this — passive production plus diffusion and decay — could never turn a percent-scale input gradient into anything close to the sharp front-versus-back contrast a moving cell actually shows. **The question the lecture poses at this point is how to amplify the signal past this passive limit.** ## Amplification by positive feedback Postma and van Haastert's answer is to add a feedback loop between the second messenger and an effector protein that shuttles between the cytosol and the membrane: - Before receptor stimulation, only a small number of (inactive) effector molecules sit on the membrane; most of the effector pool is cytosolic. - Receptor stimulation causes the membrane-bound effectors to make more of the phospholipid second messenger. - The local rise in phospholipid recruits more effector from the cytosol onto the membrane, right where the phospholipid rose — **translocation**. - That newly recruited effector lets the locally active receptor drive still more phospholipid production, at the expense of the cytosolic pool. Each step feeds the next: more local messenger recruits more local effector, which produces more local messenger. This is written by making production depend on both receptor activity and the local membrane-bound effector concentration, $$P(x) = k_o + k_E R^*(x) E_m(x),$$ where $E_m$ and $E_c$ are the membrane-bound and cytosolic effector concentrations. This positive feedback loop is what the model uses to escape the gain-less-than-one limit of the purely passive case: diffusion of the messenger plus translocation of the effector, together, can sharpen a shallow input into a much steeper, more localised response — hence "diffusion-translocation model." ## What the loop is made of, biochemically Levchenko and Iglesias's schematic identifies the actual molecules playing these roles in real chemotactic cells: receptor binding activates a heterotrimeric G-protein, which activates PI3-kinase (PI3K) — the activator, phosphorylating a membrane lipid to make PIP3 — while also activating PTEN, a phosphatase that removes that same phosphate — the inhibitor. The steady-state level of PIP3 at any point on the membrane tracks the local receptor activity $R^*$ there, and is read out by downstream proteins with pleckstrin-homology (PH) domains that bind PIP3 and are recruited to the membrane wherever it accumulates. PI3K and PTEN are the concrete activator/inhibitor pair that the abstract circuit below is meant to stand for. ## An abstract circuit for perfect adaptation Set the concrete biochemistry aside and ask what a minimal network needs in order to respond to a signal $S$ and then relax back to exactly the same steady state regardless of how large $S$ is. Such a network shows **perfect adaptation**: after a step in $S$, the output rises or falls transiently and then returns exactly to its old value, with no dependence on the new level of $S$ at steady state. The kinetics: $S$ converts an inactive pool $A$ into an active $A^*$, which decays spontaneously; symmetrically for $I \to I^*$. $A^*$ and $I^*$ then act antagonistically on a receptor pool, $A^*$ driving $R \to R^*$ and $I^*$ driving $R^* \to R$: $$\frac{dR^*}{dt} = -k_{-R} I^* R^* + k_R A^* R$$ $$\frac{dA^*}{dt} = -k_{-A} A^* + k_A' S A = -k_{-A} A^* + k_A' S (A_{tot} - A^*)$$ $$\frac{dI^*}{dt} = -k_{-I} I^* + k_I' S I = -k_{-I} I^* + k_I' S (I_{tot} - I^*)$$ The main simplifying assumption is that only a small fraction of the total activator and inhibitor pools is ever activated ($A_{tot} \gg A^*$, $I_{tot} \gg I^*$, equivalently $k_{-A}, k_{-I} \gg k_A', k_I'$). Then $A \approx A_{tot}$ and $I \approx I_{tot}$ stay essentially constant, and absorbing them into new rate constants $k_A \equiv k_A' A_{tot}$, $k_I \equiv k_I' I_{tot}$ turns the last two equations linear in $S$: $$\frac{dA^*}{dt} = -k_{-A} A^* + k_A S, \qquad \frac{dI^*}{dt} = -k_{-I} I^* + k_I S.$$ At steady state, $$A^*_{ss} = \frac{k_A}{k_{-A}} S, \qquad I^*_{ss} = \frac{k_I}{k_{-I}} S,$$ and — writing $R^*$ as the fraction of receptor active, $R + R^* = 1$ — $$R^*_{ss} = \frac{k_R A^*_{ss}/I^*_{ss}}{k_R A^*_{ss}/I^*_{ss} + k_{-R}}.$$ This is the argument for perfect adaptation: $A^*_{ss}$ and $I^*_{ss}$ are **both** proportional to $S$, so their ratio $A^*_{ss}/I^*_{ss} = (k_A/k_{-A})/(k_I/k_{-I})$ has the $S$ cancel out entirely. $R^*_{ss}$ depends on nothing but that fixed ratio, so its steady-state value is the same for every $S$ — a step up in signal changes $R^*$ only transiently, on the way to exactly the same steady state it started from. From here on, drop the stars and write $A$, $I$ for the activated species, as the lecture does. ## Adding space: one component diffuses, the rest don't The circuit above says nothing about direction — it is a single well-mixed reaction network. To get gradient sensing out of it, let only the inhibitor diffuse, while the signal $S$, the activator $A$, and the receptor $R$ stay strictly local to each point of the membrane: $$\frac{\partial I(x,t)}{\partial t} = -k_{-I} I(x,t) + k_I S(x,t) + D \frac{\partial^2 I(x,t)}{\partial x^2},$$ with a shallow linear signal across the cell, $S(x) = s_0 + s_1 x$, and no flux of $I$ out of either end of the cell — nothing to diffuse into, so nothing leaves. At steady state this reduces to a linear inhomogeneous ODE, $$\frac{\partial^2 I(x)}{\partial x^2} = \frac{k_{-I}}{D} I(x) - \frac{k_I}{D}\left(s_0 + s_1 x\right) \equiv a\,I(x) - b - c x,$$ which is exactly solvable (the lecture hands this to a computer algebra system rather than doing the integration by hand): $$I(x) = \frac{k_I}{k_{-I}}\left(s_0 + s_1\left(x - \frac{\sinh \sigma x}{\sigma} + \frac{\cosh \sigma x}{\sigma}\, \frac{\cosh \sigma - 1}{\sinh \sigma}\right)\right), \qquad \sigma \equiv \sqrt{\frac{k_{-I}}{D}}.$$ $\sigma$ is the same balance as the dispersion length from earlier, just inverted: $\sigma = 1/ \lambda_I$, where $\lambda_I = \sqrt{D/k_{-I}}$ is $I$'s own decay length. A small $\sigma$ (decay length long compared to the cell) means $I$ diffuses fast enough, relative to how fast it turns over, to average itself out across most of the cell; a large $\sigma$ means it stays close to whatever the local production dictated. (For illustration the lecture uses $k_I/k_{-I} = 1$, $s_0 = 1\ \mu\text{M}$, $s_1 = 0.1\ \mu\text{M}$, $\sigma = 0.25\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$.) ## Local excitation, global inhibition Now put the two pieces together. $A$ does not diffuse, so at every point it simply tracks the local signal exactly, $A(x) = (k_A/k_{-A})\, S(x) = (k_A/k_{-A})(s_0 + s_1 x)$ — a scaled copy of the input gradient. $I(x)$ is the smoothed solution above. From the non-spatial circuit, only the *ratio* $A/I$ matters for $R^*$ — so what the cell reads out at position $x$ is $$\frac{A(x)}{I(x)} = \frac{k_A k_{-I}}{k_{-A} k_I}\left(1 + \frac{s_1}{s_0 + s_1 x}\left(\frac{\cosh \sigma x}{\sigma}\, \frac{\cosh \sigma - 1}{\sinh \sigma} - \frac{\sinh \sigma x}{\sigma}\right) \right)^{-1},$$ which is *not* constant across the cell, even though each component individually adapts perfectly to a uniform signal. It varies with $x$ precisely because $I$ has been smoothed by diffusion while $A$ has not. The payoff is the limit of small $\sigma$ (the lecture's own example takes $\sigma \sim 0.4$): $I$ diffuses fast enough relative to its own decay to be essentially well-mixed, so it settles to the value it would have if it only ever saw the whole-cell average signal $\bar S$, $I(x) \to I(\bar S) = \text{const}$, while $A(x) = A(S(x))$ still tracks the signal exactly where it is. The readout becomes $$R^*(x) \sim \frac{A(x)}{I(x)} = \frac{A(S(x))}{I(\bar S)}$$ — **local excitation divided by global inhibition.** $A$ answers "what is the signal right here?" and the diffusing $I$ answers "what is the signal on average, over the whole cell?"; dividing the two gives a value that is large wherever the local signal exceeds the cell-wide average and small where it falls short — a readout of gradient *direction* rather than of absolute concentration. Because the whole circuit still perfectly adapts to a spatially uniform change in $S$ (shift $S$ up everywhere by the same amount and $\bar S$ shifts with it, so the ratio settles back to where it was), this readout resolves the opening problem: it distinguishes front from back without ever locking the cell into treating one absolute concentration as permanently "high." ## Sources - Slides: `computational-biology/mit-ocw/8591j/2004/lectures/20-notes/01-alternative-views-on-gradient-sensing.md` and `.../02-now-introduce-diffusion.md` (MIT OCW 8.591J, *Systems Biology*, Fall 2004, lecture 20 notes). Both files are flagged by the library as reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer — **every equation in the source carries an unverified flag** — and several figures were removed from the original slides for copyright reasons (illustrations from both papers below, and the Levchenko–Iglesias pathway schematic).
